speechtext: On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the government if the report of the auditors made necessary by the order in council of October 10 last, dealing with the equalization of the 1930 wheat pool payments on wheat, has been referred to the government, and if so, what action is the government taking.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some days ago my lion. friend told me that it was his intention to ask the question which he has just asked, and I requested him to delay until the government had had further opportunity to consider carefully its policy in this matter. I am now in position to give him an answer. The auditors' report has been referred to the government. It is the opinion of the government that the report of the auditors does not justify the government in making payment under the authority of the order in council passed on October 10, 1935. The government is of the opinion, however, that in view of the policies followed under the previous government in handling, the 1930 wheat pool surplus, the producers of wheat who accepted an initial payment of fifty cents a bushel or fifty-five cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, are justified in expecting those payments to be equalized at sixty cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William. It is, therefore, the intention of the government to have legislation introduced without delay to provide for the equalization of the 1930 pool payments on wheat at sixty cents a bushel basis No. 1 northern, Fort William.
On the orders of the day:

I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret). Has the government decided what leave of absence is to be granted to the returned men employed in the public service who wish to take advantage of the proposed pilgrimage to Vimy this year?

Mr. Speaker, I desire to thank the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of his question. On January 10, 1936, an order in council was passed dealing with the granting of special leave with pay to ex-soldier civil servants and their immediate relatives who are eligible to take part in the Vimy and battlefields pilgrimage in 1936, and who desire to do so. The order in council provides that eleven days be added as special leave with pay to the three weeks usually allowed as statutory leave, such special leave not -to be counted as a charge against the employee's special leave credit. The order in council further empowers the deputy heads of departments to grant such additional time as may be necessary for travelling to and from the point of embarkation. The point was raised as to whether this was intended to apply only to civil servants who are under the Civil Service Act. I may say the intention is that the order in council shall apply to all civil servants, whether they are under the
Civil Service Act or not.

Dealers:	General letter No. 12. Repair
prices for ball and roller bearings, bolts, nuts, washers, screws and rivets-

I do not think the hon.
gentleman should read the letter; he should put his question directly.

I must read the letter in
order to make my question intelligible. It is a very short letter.

I do not think the hon.

This letter indicates that
effective immediately the prices of parts necessary for duty free farm tractors will be increased 33i per cent. The letter states that this increase in price is made necessary on account of duty now being paid on these parts. Could the minister advise whether there has been any increase in the duty on parts necessary for duty free tractors? If
there has not been any increase, will the government take some action in regard to this increase in the price of parts which are so important to the farmers of western Canada?

Health of animals, administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $1,900,400.

Mr. Chairman, I have thought sometimes that the manner in which these agriculture estimates are brought down is such that they do not convey as much information to the committee as they should convey if we are to have an intelligent discussion. Quite a large sum is involved in this item, and it would add very much to the conduct of debate if the minister would state briefly why these expenditures are to be made and what particular functions are performed by this branch of the department.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
It will be noted that the estimates submitted for the year 1936-37 show a slight increase over those of 1935-36, the total esti-

mate being increased by $12,484. The different purposes for which this money is to be expended are:
Communication of services, $14,050,
Equipment, acquisition and maintenance,

Compensation, largely having to do with the checking of tuberculosis in cattle throughout the country, $413,937.
Lands, buildings, acquisition and maintenance, $6,500.
Miscellaneous current expenses, $13,300.
Personal services in connection with staffs, $1,120,693.
Special personal services, $1,100.
Kents. $10,220.
Supplies, materials, printing, stationery, etc., $54,000.
Transportation of things, $6,600.
Transportation and travelling expenses of persons, $249,000.
Is it the intention to bring any new areas under the tuberculosis test this year?

Yes. There is the new area in New Brunswick, which I think completes the bringing of that province into the district there. Then there is a new area in Ontario, taking in certain counties around Toronto, from the county of Northumberland through to the county of Halton. There are three new areas in Manitoba, and there are under consideration one or two others that have not yet been passed upon.

In view of the serious epidemic which occurred among horses in western Canada at the end of August and in September this year, has any additional provision been made in this particular estimate to deal with that matter?

It is the opinion of the department that that was a disease which was due partly to conditions on both sides of the international boundary-that is, the drought conditions that have prevailed for a number of years. We do not expect that there will be any new outbreak this year and therefore there is no provision for it. Of course, that is something that would have to be dealt with at the time if it developed.

What is the policy of the government regarding the checking of tuberculosis in dairy herds throughout the country? That is a vital question to which more attention should be paid. A closer check should be kept on dairy herds, because I believe a great deal of milk offered for sale to-day comes from diseased herds.

There are three different schemes for checking tuberculosis generally.

There is the accredited herd system; there is the restricted area policy in which all cattle are checked over the whole area; and there is the supervised herd plan. In connection with the first two the government pays compensation for stock destroyed, but it does not in connection with the third. All these plans are applied in the attempt to eradicate tuberculosis from dairy and other herds throughout the country.
I have in mind particularly the anti-tuberculosis area in the Fraser valley district. What percentage of reactors was there in the last test, or is that district cleaned up completely?

I do not know that it can be said that any district has 'been entirely cleaned up, but the trouble has been reduced to such an extent in some districts that the reactors are only one-half of one per cent of the cattle tested, which shows that there has been a marked diminution in the disease in the different districts. The reduction sometimes has been from five per cent to one-half of one per cent, and in other instances from an even higher percentage. There has been a considerable reduction as a result of the policy.
Is it the policy of the government to extend the testing system further than it has been carried in the past? In my opinion it has not covered the ground as it should.

My information is that the maritime provinces, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, are now restricted areas; that is, they have been set out as an area in which an attempt is being made to eradicate tuberculosis. The government is extending areas in other provinces as rapidly as the funds available will make this possible. The efforts of the department are limited only by the amount of money which this house sees fit to vote from time to time to take care of that matter.
Is the amount to be voted for indemnity for cattle in connection with the tuberculosis test more or less than it was last year?
The total amount is $6,063 less than it was last year.

In my district a disease, not new but one that has become prevalent within the last two or three years, needs looking into. It is known as shipping fever, the

Supply-Agriculture
technical name being hemorrhagic septicaemia. It is a very infectious disease and has resulted in a good many fatalities among herds that have been infected. Has any notice been taken of it by the department? If so, what is being done to eliminate it?

The department is not touching it. It is an infection that is widespread throughout the country and one that is somewhat difficult to deal with, but the department is not dealing with it at the moment.
Is the bacteriological department taking no steps at all to investigate the matter?

The information of the department is that the disease is due usually to bad handling of stock and to poor feeding. It is a disease that is likely to develop in connection with the shipment of cattle, and likely to develop anywhere. Investigations have been made, and it is generally considered to be caused by bad handling and poor feeding, and of course that cause can be removed only by more education among the people in connection with feeding and shipping conditions.

A good many of the cases that have come under my notice have been contracted while cattle were being shipped on railway cars. Even at the Toronto exhibition cattle have been infected with the disease, with serious consequences. If the department have not taken any steps towards investigating the matter I advise that they do so, because I believe the disease is spreading, and it is very serious, in some districts at least.
I shall be very pleased to take the matter up with the department.
With respect to the question I raised a few moments ago, the minister said it was considered in the United States and Canada that this was a drought disease among horses.
Not exactly a drought disease, but one that develops as a result of conditions of hardship that prevail in the area.

I was just going to ask the minister if he is aware of the fact that this disease was quite prevalent in the districts around Rosetown where drought had not been particularly severe, and what steps were being taken to study it. I think it is something that should be watched very carefully by the department.

I would only say in reply that it just depends upon how large an area the member for Rosetown-Biggar would take in around Rosetown. He says there have been no drought conditions around Rosetown. My information is that the drought conditions extended north, south, east and west of Rosetown, and of course you would have the development of any disease that resulted from that in areas which were comparatively small, where they might have fairly good crops. Right around Rosetown it is fairly true that in some years, when we have had drought elsewhere, the crop has been comparatively good, but parts of that district have been very much affected.
I said "not particularly" affected. Does the minister or the department consider that this is an infectious or contagious disease?
The department is inclined to think that it is not contagious, but it is not in a position to state definitely. The disease has not been confirmed by those who have been investigating.
Is it the policy of the government to test dairy herds upon application of the farmers, irrespective of the number of pure bred animals that may be in that herd?
The supervised herd plan takes any number at all, but the accredited herd plan requires that five of the live stock be pure bred.

I think that, in checking up on disease, to limit them to five pure bred cattle is a mistake. There are many splendid grade herds in the country, and it is just as important that the milk coming from a grade herd should be pure as that coming from a pure bred herd.

What provision is made to protect consumers against disease in cattle that have been butchered? Oftentimes they are butchered outside and peddled in the town. I know of cases where that has been done, with very serious consequences.
That is handled under public health in the different provinces.

Will the minister find it possible to establish a tubercular zone over the Porcupine and Cochrane area-most of the northern area? This is very important on account of the amount of milk that is being used in that section.
Supply-Agriculture
In order to have that done it will be necessary in the first place for two-thirds of the cattle men in that area to petition the government to make that an area.
They have done that.

And after that is done the matter is investigated by the department, and if sufficient funds are available other areas are added as we think it is necessary to add them. At the moment I think that what are already in will require practically all the money that is being voted in this fund. I am informed by the officials of the department that there is no petition in from that area.

It is very important that this should be done. The minister will readily understand what it means. In a section of the country where the farmers are really established farmers they get compensation for their losses; but in most cases around the mining areas they are beginners, and when this disease occurs they do not get any compensation whatever: it is a dead loss to those settlers. Their plight is a very different one from what you will find in the older settled sections of Ontario, Quebec and other provinces. The minister will understand that it is impossible to bring raw milk in from outside, from Toronto for instance. We have to produce milk around these mining sections, and the minister will appreciate the plight of these poor settlers when the whole of their cattle have to be destroyed.

Have any steps yet been taken to give effect to recommendations made in the report of the price spreads and mass buying commission in connection with the administration of the Meat and Canned Foods Act? It will be recalled it was discovered that certain abuses existed, not only abuses but perhaps inadequate standards and provisions for containers. I am referring now particularly to canned goods, although reference is made also to other classes of goods. On page 241 of the report, dealing with this question of grading and so on, I find these words:
Nowhere are simple numerical grades used for consumer products, and even in one of the best grading systems, that of canned foods, the grade names do not indicate in themselves the position of any one grade in the series. These designations are "fancy quality," "choice quality," "standard1 quality" and "second quality"; "second quality" being, in fact, fourth grade.
It goes on to say, elaborating that a little further:
It is recommended that all grade designations be numerical, as grade 1, grade 2, etc. Should this prove impossible for some products, alphabetical grades might be used, as with eggs for export trade.

Referring to the question of grading canned goods, it has been noticed, and I think commented upon quite widely by those who are interested, that the use of those terms, "fancy," "choice," and so forth, is really meaningless, that there ought to be a standard; and I believe in the department the officers or the inspectors have certain standards. I am not for a moment complaining about those standards, nor am I criticizing the department in respect of its examination of the goods. What I am calling attention to is what we discovered on that occasion, and as I say it has been widely commented upon, that the consumer may be very easily grossly misled. Furthermore it constitutes an unfair competition between different manufacturers. A given manufacturer may have an article which he describes as "choice," "fancy," or something else. What is required in the interests of the consumer is that in canned fruits, canned peaches if you like, or strawberries, there shall be a standard No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 or No. 4 grade, as the case may be, and that these numerical descriptions be set forth in clear, outstanding type which will indicate clearly to the consumer the standard that is being sold. I know perfectly well from my knowlege of the subject that often a secondary grade, known to the departmental officials as secondary, is described on the label in such a way that an ordinary purchaser could not possibly understand that he was buying a secondary grade, and he might really be, and in fact often is, deceived into thinking he is getting a really superior article. And inasmuch as there are different types of labels and descriptions by different firms the competition of price becomes the main competition while actually there may be a great deal of unfairness in connection with the quality.
On that point-and there are other points to which I shall refer later-I should like to ask the minister if any steps have been taken since last session, when the price spreads report was presented to this parliament, to carry out the suggestions contained in that report or to correct the present practice, which in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of many others, is more or less deceptive to the consumer.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member will agree when I say that some of the matters he has brought forward and the question he has asked would have to be considered not only by the Department of Agriculture but also by the Department of Health. Most of the questions asked by my hon. friend really have to do with another vote so far as they concern agriculture; that is the vote having to do with canned goods.

Supply-Agriculture
I wish to place myself right; this vote refers to the Meat and Canned Foods Act.

Yes. Of course meat would naturally come under this item, but I think most of my hon. friend's questions had to do with canned vegetables and canned fruit. However, I do not object to giving him the information now; I am just directing attention to that fact. The only reply I can make is that the different branches of the Department of Agriculture, together with the Health department and others concerned, have been giving consideration to those recommendations, and an effort is being made to work out some better plan of grading and marking which will meet as far as possible the recommendations of the committee. Nothing definite has been done up to the moment, but the whole matter is under consideration.

There is another point
to which I should like to direct attention; that is, the sizes of packages. I think this is one of the most flagrant abuses prevalent in the distribution trade to-day. Passing along the street-you can see it in Ottawa as you can see it everywhere else-I frequently see advertised in the windows, usually of a chain store, certain articles, canned meat, canned tomatoes or any article of common use, at a price that is startlingly low. It is very skilfully done; the inference is that this particular institution is able to sell canned tomatoes, we will say, at a price much below its competitors. Then passing along the street I have seen in another window, of a competing store-perhaps an independent merchant-a can of tomatoes that seems to be exactly the same size, but the price of which is two or three cents higher. Immediately the unsuspecting purchaser will note the question of price, and of course he is drawn to the first store. On examination of the cans, however, it will be found that one is half an inch shorter than the other. Half an inch is not readily discernible to the unpractised eye, but it means a difference of perhaps ten per cent, which of course means that in one can you get ten per cent less than in the other, and therefore the price, although it appears to be lower, may be just the same, possibly higher or perhaps very slightly lower.
Again this is a deceptive thing. My own view, frankly and candidly, is that it was designed to deceive, because it was introduced only a few years ago. Formerly there were standard sizes, although I do not know that there was a law or statute forcing merchants to sell only certain sizes. By common practice over the years, however, certain sizes 12739-is
were accepted and recognized. The old size for tomatoes was a two pound tin, if my memory serves me aright. Now you can buy tomatoes in a number of different sizes, and I am convinced that this is a flagrant abuse. I may say further that the evidence before the committee two years ago, and I think before the commission last year, indicated that some of these large and powerful distributing agencies or institutions were able to buy a certain standard article in a size slightly smaller than the size furnished to others, and this size container was prepared especially for them. Later I believe the same privilege was extended to others, but at first undoubtedly it gave the one institution that was successful in getting the special size a distinct advantage over its competitors. It was a deceptive thing; it was not fair competition, and the consumer obtained no advantage.
There is another form that it takes. What I have said applies particularly to canned goods, but let us consider bottled jam. I do not know whether samples are available now, but samples were available which demonstrated that a bottle of jam was put up in such shape and form that it appeared to contain actually more than it did. It was scientifically designed to deceive the eye, without doubt; in fact it was one of the triumphs of science, the optical illusion that was created by just looking at the jar. Yet the net contents of that jar were very much less than those of a jar used by a competitor.
The minister will please accept this assurance from me, that I am not directing these remarks in any sense as a criticism of his administration of the department; this is a question for parliament, but at the moment he is responsible for the administration of this part of the country's affairs. To my mind it is the duty of parliament to see to it that no such deception is allowed, that that practice is eliminated. There should be standardization of sizes of bottles for jam and of cans for canned goods so that there may at least be some uniformity. I think it would surprise the minister to know what a great variety of sizes there is. For canned fruits and vegetables, peas, corn, tomatoes, peaches, plums, strawberries, about two sizes would be ample to cover the requirements of the trade. This variety of sizes is not in any sense a contribution to efficiency in merchandising. I do not think anyone here who has had experience in merchandising would say I am wrong in that. I am convinced that there is but one object in having this variety of sizes, and that is the object of cajoling-or I would use a stronger term, deceiving-the consumer. I

Supply-Agriculture

am willing to make all reasonable allowance to the minister for the short time he has been in office, but after all, these things were brought out two years ago, and while I am not inclined to press any criticism of the minister I suggest to him that the permanent officials responsible for the administration of these acts might well, shall I say, be brought to task, or at least be asked to explain why they have not made to their minister recommendations for the elimination of this kind of deception practised upon the consumer on the one hand and constituting on the other hand a grossly unfair form of competition. I strongly urge upon the minister the necessity of early and prompt action for the correction of these matters.

I appreciate the attitude of the hon. member towards myself as the present head of the department. I can assure him that I am informed by the officials of the department during the short time I have been its head that consideration is being given to the matters he has brought before the committee this afternoon. Again it is a question of dealing with two departments, that of trade and commerce, which my hon. friend understands much better than I do, having himself been in charge of it for a considerable time, and, since we are charged with the administration of the act, the department of which at the moment I happen to be the head. As I said in regard to the other matter so I say in regard to this, that it is under consideration at the moment. I have much in common with my hon. friend in the views I hold in regard to the methods that have been followed in the putting up of packages. Of course I do not know what was the intention of those who first put food products up in these packages. Many people who purchase from chain and other stores where these goods are sold have known for a considerable time that the packages are not as large as some of those purchased in other places at higher prices. There are different reasons why persons purchase smaller packages, I need not discuss that; but it is the desire of the department and of myself as its head that everything which tends to deceive the public should be done away with, and that as quickly as possible. So far as I have charge of the department that will be done.

The minister referred to the fact that for some years I was presiding over the Department of Trade and Commerce. I imagine he inferred I might have done something while I was there. The long and short of it is that it illustrates a clash of

jurisdiction. When I was minister I sought urgently and strenuously to get some action, and I tell the minister frankly I could get no action because of the attitude of the Department of Agriculture. I am not desirous of going into any discussion of that phase of the situation, but it indicates this-and that is one reason I am glad that I am addressing a minister who comes fresh to his task-that the administration should be in the hands of either one department or the other; there should not be this clash of jurisdiction. I am certain the interdepartmental correspondence will show that the permanent officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce have long been of the opinion that there is need for amendments to the act. If the Prime Minister were in his seat-for after all it is the Prime Minister who must decide on matters where there is a dual responsibility-I would appeal to him to give consideration to that phase of the subject, so that there can be no evasion of responsibility.
There is another abuse that I wish to emphasize. The department in the administration of these acts requires that the net weight be shown on the label, but I invite any hon. member whose family is keeping house to go into the kitchen, pick up any canned goods and look at the minute figures in which the weight of the contents is shown -16 ounces, 14, 13, or whatever it may be; the figures should be clear and such as can be read. Furthermore, as this report suggests, they should do away entirely with these odd weights such as 14 1-2 or 13 ounces. The report definitely suggests that the quantity should be 4, 8, or 16 ounces, definite divisions of what the housewife knows as a pound, not 15 ounces, for instance-there was that size; I do not know whether it is still put out-and 14 and 12 ounces.
May I refer to another point in this report which I think is very important. I commend this particularly to the attention of the minister :
It is our opinion that legislative provision should be made for the standardization by order in council of the quantities in which any packaged commodity, whether a food product or not, may be sold.
And that the act should be amended accordingly. I believe the practice at present is this-and I invite the minister to correct me if I state it inaccurately; I am speaking from memory, nearly all these provisions are made by regulation under order in council. I am not one of those who seek, and I am not seeking now, to tie the hands of the administration, but I do think we sometimes

Supply-A griculture
lean towards an abuse of that privilege. There are certain things that might well be statutory. The act might very clearly state, for instance, that there shall not be more than such and such a number of sizes, or, as I mentioned a moment ago, that all grades 6hall be designated numerically, one, two, three, four, and so forth, or A, B, C, D, et cetera. Furthermore, we might clearly provide by statute that there shall not be any division of a pound except as indicated here, 2 ounces, 4, 6, 8 ounces, and so forth. These are things that could be fixed by statute. I am anxious, Mr. Chairman, that what I have to say shall not be lost on the desert air.
I am listening.

I am afraid the minister
is listening with one ear and talking with the other.
Are you sure you are not?

I say that the statute ought to determine many of these things, and then the governor in council would be limited in the powers he has for stretching the regulations to cover a variety of things such as I have dealt with. I would very earnestly plead with the minister that in connection with this whole subject the recommendations of the price spreads commission should be given careful consideration and an effort made to eliminate these abuses. I am quite aware that the various acts we now have contain elaborate provisions respecting a variety of matters, but these abuses are obviously present, and it is our duty in the face of past experience so to amend the act as to eliminate them if possible.

Mr. Chairman, I was a
member of the Toronto board of health for some years and I saw something of the enforcement of these acts. I would ask the minister to tell the committee what cooperation or coordination there is between his department and provincial health officers regarding the administration of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and the Meat and Canned Foods Act. We have had many complaints about canned goods, about the cheap stuff that is worked off on the working class. The city of Toronto and the county of York have spent a large sum of money in setting up a modem health department. What is this parliament doing? The government proposes to spend SI,900.000 on the health of animals and only one-fifth of that amount on the health of human beings. It is a wonderful country, Canada, is it not? I agree with the former Minister of Trade 12739-181
and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that there is a great deal of inefficiency in the administration of these acts. Every person who has been interested in public health must know that there are abuses. When I first served on the board of health in Toronto there was no health inspection, although there was some kind of inspection of food. But the great Doctor Hastings, former medical officer of the city of Toronto, was responsible for having the milk supply of the city of Toronto inspected for sixty miles around the city, and that operated for the welfare of the people of Toronto, children especially, and helped to cut down contagious diseases among animals. I think the minister should	tell the	committee what he intends to do to provide for a more efficient administration of these acts. I was told by one health inspector that you could not enforce	the	act.	He said	"thefederal department	has	taken	it over now."That is how they	get	away	with it.	The
chain stores sell cheap and they dump canned goods into their windows. Prosecutions in Toronto are few and far between, although a lot of these goods are afterwards found by the street cleaning departments. I agree with the former minister that there is great inefficiency, and a lack of cooperation and coordination between the federal department and the public health officials in the large cities. There is room for much improvement in that direction, and I think the minister ought to call a conference of the health officers of the large cities throughout the country with a view to bringing about closer cooperation and coordination.
Then as to prosecutions, we were told last session by the Minister of Justice that all federal law enforcement is in the provinces, and that the federal department has nothing to do with federal prosecutions. I was told a few sessions ago to see the attorney general of the province. I would like to find out what the minister proposes to do along this line. The enforcement of all these acts under the Department of Agriculture should be the duty of the minister, who should see that prosecutions by him are instituted in Toronto and other police courts for violations of the acts. The summons is laid under the act, but the person in charge of the summons has no power. He is only a food inspector for a municipality, and the result is that the consumer is getting the worst of it. I sympathize with the producer because he is having a hard time of it in many ways, but here we are dealing with the health of our people, and we have this government spending only 8475,000 on the health of human beings and 81,900,000 on the health of animals.

Is that Canada's conception of the worth of human beings, many of whom are unable to get employment and some of whom are starving? Yet the government appoints inspectors, and inspectors of inspectors, and inspectors of inspectors of those who are the chief inspectors. What they do I do not know. There is a great lack of coordination between the health officers in the cities and this department, and it is these local health officers who are most familiar with the situation. They are local men, right on the ground, and they know the conditions in the abattoirs where cattle are killed and where the food is put into cans. They know the operations of the canning companies. The late government did a great thing for public health when it appointed the price spreads commission, and the work of that commission was most commendable from the point of view of public health. If the minister wants a proper administration of these acts he should coordinate with the medical officers of health and with the police departments or police chiefs of the large cities, and his inspectors should see that there is an efficient inspection. Probably the minister has not been long enough in the department to become familiar with it or to do much as yet, but I hope that in the recess he will visit Toronto and try to bring about closer cooperation between the local boards of health in the province and police officials and federal officials so that the consumer will get some benefit from the expenditure of these large sums of money.

Is the minister prepared to inform the committee what the policy of his department will be regarding pullorum disease in chickens? It is rather a serious matter in British Columbia, and I know that the minister has received representations from a number of people. I have made them myself, but so far without any reply. I hope others have been more successful. The present regulations are founded apparently upon the belief, which is contradicted by some people claiming authority, that the disease is wholly hereditary, and so we are not allowed to sell our day-old chicks in Al'berta or Saskatchewan or anywhere outside the province unless we can produce the pedigree of the chicks' fathers and mothers and aunts and uncles to quite a remote degree. This is very expensive.
There are three complaints made in British Columbia of the manner in which these regulations are enforced. First, the complaint is made that it is very expensive and is calculated to injure the laying qualities of the

birds. It puts them off their laying, and when a bird has been put off its laying it is a long time before it gets back again. It is alleged also that there is another method, known as the quick method, which does not have this effect. This need not be carried out by government inspectors, but can be done by the poultry owner himself at a tenth of the cost. It is claimed that this method is equally effective. The poultry men want to know, and I do not think they will be quiet until they do know, why the more modern, cheaper and *equally effective method has not been adopted. Special provision was made last year, probably on account of the trouble which arose, under which the dominion government paid part of the expenses, but that was only an emergent action.
The second complaint is in connection with the contention that this disease is an hereditary disease. I have seen articles in some of the poultry journals by people who claim to know, contradicting the idea that this disease is wholly of an hereditary character. It is said that too much emphasis is being placed upon that phase of the matter. It is claimed that the diseases may be contracted because of local conditions, because of poor surroundings or improper sanitation, and so on, and that it is not entirely an hereditary disease. The regulations are based entirely upon the idea that the disease is hereditary, that it is conveyed from father to son or from mother to daughter, so to speak. The results of these regulations have been very injurious to the poultry industry in British Columbia. In the past the price of eggs has been low and the price of feed from the prairies has been high. These things have mitigated against the success of these men, and yet the government comes along, no doubt with the best intentions, and states that they must conform to certain regulations before they can sell their day-old chicks. A great many people have been forced out of the business. Not only has it been necessary to test the parents of the chicks, but it has been necessary to test the more remote relations; the whole flock has had to be tested. It is an expensive procedure and the benefits are doubtful. There is another method known as the quick method by which a drop of blood is taken from the chicken and a test made immediately. The laying qualities of the bird and its general health are not interfered with.
This matter is of great importance to British Columbia. I was unable to get a reply from the department as to what their policy would be and the only thing left for me

Suppl y-A griculture
to do was to bring up the matter here. I know the minister has not been long in office and has not had time to familiarize himself with every detail of this branch, but I ask him to undertake to look into the matter to see if some redress cannot be given to the poultry owners of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, there
has been considerable correspondence from British Columbia with regard to the difficulties to which the hon. member (Mr. Neill) has just referred. I may say that these regulations were really set up as a result of the activities of the live stock branch, under which hatcheries are controlled. However, I think it would be just as well to deal with this matter at this time as we have been discussing live stock diseases generally. The general impression in the department, an impression pretty well established by experience, is that this disease is not wholly hereditary, but rather it is one which is transmitted by infection. The objective of the department is to try to prevent the spreading of the disease. The regulations set up do not automatically come into force in the different parts of Canada; they are made applicable in a province only when that province asks that they be applied. The three prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and two of the maritime provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, have applied to have these regulations put into force within their boundaries. As I understand them, the regulations require that any one who is supplying eggs to a hatchery, the chicks from which are going to be sold to the public, is required to have all his hens blood .tested. Objection to these regulations has been taken in British Columbia. That province has not asked that these regulations shall apply there, and in so far as chicks sold within the province are concerned, the regulations do not apply. However, when they undertake to sell chicks in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, or the eastern provinces of New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, they are affected by the regulations.
At the time of the dominion-provincial conference Alberta intimated that they had no objection to chicks being shipped into Alberta provided that the hens in the flock used for hatchery purposes were segregated from those not used for hatchery purposes. In other words, if a poultryman has 1,000 hens of which only 300 are used for hatchery purposes, if he segregates those 300 and has them tested, Alberta is prepared to accept chicks that are hatched from eggs laid by those particular hens. Saskatchewan and Manitoba insist that the entire flock shall be tested, as regards both chicks raised and
sold within the province and chicks brought in from outside. British Columbia is, therefore, excluded from selling chicks in Saskatchewan or Manitoba, unless such chicks are raised from eggs taken from flocks all the hens of which have been blood tested.
The whole flock.

Yes, the whole flock
blood tested. I understand that in some cases, probably in all cases, this has raised the cost to the poultryman. Some misunderstanding has arisen between the poultrymen of British Columbia and the department administering these particular regulations. Everything possible is being done to have the regulations applied in all provinces in order that a disease which has been affecting poultrymen everywhere may be eradicated with the least possible cost to the individuals concerned.

The minister has shown a
very thorough knowledge of this subject, but there is one point upon which he did not touch. He stated that Alberta and Saskatchewan demand that imported chicks comply with the regulations, but he did not state that these regulations were formulated at Ottawa and Alberta and Saskatchewan had to accept them holus-bolus. If they wanted certain tests applied, the only way they could get them was by adopting the dominion formulated rules. If the dominion rules were less stringent, or, as we might say in British Columbia, more reasonable, Alberta and Saskatchewan would still adopt them and the situation would be eased. These rules were formulated by the dominion at a time when the officials were less informed about the matter, and it was decided that this longer and more expensive method should be used; but since that time there has been devised a quicker test which can be carried out instantly by taking a drop of blood from the bird. Not only is this test cheaper, but it is less dangerous. If the dominion would change its rules I am sure Alberta and Saskatchewan would adopt them; as a matter of fact they would have to adopt them. If the minister would look into this point I think he would see where many of our objections could be met.

In the short experience I have had in the department, I did take into consideration, at the request of British Columbia, the change that has been suggested by the hon. member; but I found very quickly, after attempting to make that suggestion to the other provinces, that the pressure is coming not from Ottawa but from those provinces; that is, they absolutely refuse to

be governed by any other regulations than those to which they now conform and which they regard as proper regulations. I still have some doubt as to whether exactly the same rules should govern in all cases in view of the differing conditions. Saskatchewan is a province where most of the poultry producers are also farmers in a rather large way, and their problem is perhaps somewhat different from that of the man who makes his whole livelihood out of the production of poultry. To begin with, they have smaller flocks and it is probably not a matter of great expense to them to have the test made that is now being carried out. On the other side of the question, however, I am informed by those who have knowledge of the subject that the quick test is only approximately forty per cent effective. This test was known at the time the other one was accepted, and it was known at that time to be only approximately forty per cent effective. Of course, it is the desire of the department as far as possible to eliminate disease, and we take the most effective means to that end. Consideration might be given to some changes in the regulations as we gain further experience, by segregating hens in such a manner as to make the test effective, but up to date we have nothing more effective than we are now doing.

I agree with the minister heartily as to the desirability of having baby chicks hatched from eggs coming from blood-tested flocks, for it is very desirable indeed that disease should be stamped out as quickly as possible. But there is another question in this connection that seems to me to be of great importance to the poultry industry. Under the terms of the trade agreement now in effect between Canada and the United States, the hatcheries of Canada will be subject beyond question to very severe competition with chicks coming from that country. I do not know how the department is going to see to it that chicks coming from the United States come from blood-tested flocks. I should be glad if he would explain how that will be done, or why the people of the different provinces in Canada should be subjected to this way of doing things while eggs and particularly chicks are allowed to come from the United States without undergoing that inspection and supervision.

I can only say that we are governed more or less by the action of the provinces. For example, in the provinces I have mentioned, where these regulations have been adopted, it is a comparatively simple matter to make arrangements at ports

of entry for a check to be made on the hatcheries from which chicks come, and with regard to the regulations governing them in the United States. But in a province which has not come under these regulations it is more difficult to control the situation, as one can understand. As regards the other question, under the tariff arrangements as they were before, I think the set price from the United States, upon which the tariff was based, was about 30 cents a chick. Of course, the price of a chick in the United States is around 5 cents, while on this side it is 8, 10 or 12 cents, and it can be readily seen that a set price of 30 cents would be prohibitive. In connection with the trade agreement, under the intermediate tariff, the duty on a chick coming across the line is about 5 cents.
Is that settled yet?

No, I beg your pardon; there is an ad valorem of 17 per cent based on the price, which probably in some instances, on the lower priced chicks, would figure out at a little lower than one cent a chick. Chicks would come across the line under that arrangement much more freely than they did under the previous system, but the request that has been made by the hatchery people is that a definite duty of so much per chick be imposed, and the rate suggested is very much lower than that proposed before. The house is not bound, even if the trade agreement is accepted, to abide by the present rate; we have the power to raise the duty or to do whatever we wish to do in connection with it. That, however, is a matter which I cannot discuss this afternoon; it is something that will have to be discussed when the budget is down. Representations have been made by the hatchery people to have a change of rate on chicks from the United States.

Has the department
considered making it compulsory to grade farm products packed for export and, if approved, to have them so marked?

I do not know how
far afield I am allowed to go under the rules in discussing this item. That is a mattgr entirely outside the items we are now considering, and perhaps the hon. gentleman would let it stand until a more appropriate time.

minister and those hon. members who have spoken with regard to the poultry question for the excellent information which has been given the committee and recorded in Han-

sard. This is a matter that closely affects my own constituents in Nanaimo. I am pleased that I shall be able to pass on to them from the proceedings in this committee much valuable information.

May I supplement the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) with reference to the question of inspection. I do not think that any direct answer has been given by the minister. It was my privilege a short time ago to go' through one of the packing houses in Toronto and I observed then that a great many carcasses were being rejected on account of tuberculosis. My hon. friend has referred to cooperation between the federal and provincial departments. As regards carcasses that are stamped as completely affected by tuberculosis, does the minister feel sure that the provincial department of health is cooperating to the extent of preventing these carcasses from reaching the hamburger and hot dog stands or finding their way into the canned goods sold in Ontario and throughout the dominion?

Replying first to the last question, I can assure the hon. gentleman that carcasses condemned by the dominion inspectors go into the tank immediately, under the supervision of the officials of the department. In connection with the other matter brought up by the hon. member for Broadview, and which has been referred to by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart), I would point out that under the British North America Act the matter of health comes within provincial jurisdiction. We have really very little legal control in that regard. The department, however, has always assumed that one of its main duties is to see to it as far as possible that commodities produced in this country can be sold abroad. For that reason we have attempted in the first place to keep our live stock particularly clear of disease, because other countries will not admit that live stock if disease is prevalent here. The same idea has followed into the matter of killing and the inspecting of abattoirs where meat is killed, and in the matter of canning and all that sort of thing. As a matter of choice, most of the abattoirs in Canada do require inspection by the department. The department make that inspection; they pass the meats that go out from the abattoirs, and municipalities and provinces alike have the benefit of that inspection. But when it comes to a matter of enforcing the law in that regard, it is in a little different field, and in some cases we are not in a position to act as suggested by the hon. member for Broadview. There are certain things that probably we could not do, that we would have to leave to the municipalities and the provinces, because we have not the authority to enforce. But we have followed the practice of going just as far as we can possibly go in cooperating with municipalities. Probably I should put it the other way round: we have been going as far as the constitution, the laws and regulations of the provinces and municipalities themselves, and the cooperation of abattoirs and people interested in marketing their meats will go, in order to try to enforce all over Canada the same kind of regulation in connection with the marketing of these products. I think probably the best answer I can give as to whether or not we have that cooperation is the fact that the great percentage of the meat that is going out from these abattoirs is government inspected. That would indicate that municipal bodies, provincial governments and the abattoirs themselves are inviting cooperation from the federal government in seeing to it that any meats that are sold to the public are meats that are fit for human consumption.

That covers the matter of carcasses that are going out for consumption over the retail counter. But is the minister sure they do not go into canned products and things of that kind? That was the point I was more concerned about.
Well, that would not be possible in any of the plants where inspection is carried out by the federal government. With regard to some others, it may be.

Is it not a fact that in the inspected abattoirs, for example, when hogs are slaughtered and there is found to be disease in the heads of the hogs, the heads alone are condemned and the carcasses are sold for human consumption.
Yes; with regard to certain diseases, where local infection takes place, that would be true.

Are the same standards of health required for meat that goes into cans as for meat sold by the carcass? May I point out that canned meats were imported into this country last year equivalent, I believe, to some twenty thousand head of cattle. What supervision and inspection, if any, are undertaken when that class of goods comes into the country?

Official certificates are
supplied from the governments of those countries, just as we have to supply official certifi-

cates from this country to other countries. We get the same kind of official certificate as others require of us. which gives just as good security as we can possibly have in respect of these countries.

Is it not also a fact
that if farmers bring into these inspected areas carcasses that are in any particular diseased, the whole of the carcass is destroyed? Why should not the government enforce the regulations upon the big packers as well as upon the farmers?

May I get the intent
of the hon. member's question? Has it to do with carcasses brought in?

Carcasses slaughtered
on the farms, say, and brought in for consumption in an area where there is inspection.
They are under exactly the same regulations as the abattoirs.

I do not see just how
that can be. If part of the carcass is diseased the whole of it is destroyed should it come from the farm into the city. I believe that to be the case from my own association with a municipal body where we went into this problem very carefully. One of the reasons why we did not adopt meat inspection was just exactly the one to which I have referred. If the animal is slaughtered in the abattoir, then, in the case of certain diseases, only the part of the carcass affected is destroyed. I wonder if the government has considered the making of regulations to ensure equality to all concerned.

I am informed that the regulations in so far as they are applied here are the same. Of course there may be regulations in towns and cities or provinces that I cannot speak of from this place at the moment.

What is the official disposition of a condemned or diseased carcass? The minister made the remark a moment ago that it went into the tank. I am not sure, and many who are not familiar with the butcher business do not know, just what that means. Is it put in there to purify it before it is sold? The thing I am particularly interested in is the final disposition of a condemned carcass.
It is put into tanks and rendered, and as I understand it, it is not used for human consumption. Most of it goes for fertilizer.

I asked the minister a
question a short time ago, and I want to pursue it because of the two questions that have been asked. In replying to the questions the minister dealt with meat going over the retail counter and meat going into cans, but what about cattle that have been condemned for dairy purposes and a strong suspicion remains in the mind of the government veterinary that it has been butchered and peddled through the town? Of course he has no authority to act, but is there any way by which the matter can be reported to the provincial and municipal authorities and be taken care of? I know of government men who have strongly suspected that that was going on, but it is not within their jurisdiction to do anything about it.
Provincial and municipal.

I was wondering if the
machinery set up could be correlated so that that could be taken care of. It is not the function of the man in charge, and yet it is a tremendous menace to the public health.

Before this item carries I
would like to ask the minister a question that has often been asked of me. Is it the intention of the government to investigate the prevalence of Bang's disease? Following that up, is it their intention to carry out tests, and if the cattle are found diseased, to slaughter them, and will the owners of the slaughtered animals be compensated as in the case of tuberculosis?

The department has
been investigating the spread of Bang's disease and has been doing a good deal in order to check its spread among cattle. As a matter of fact as I understand it we would be compelled to do so, whether we desired to or not, 'because of regulations particularly in the United States with regard to the export of cattle. All the cattle that are shipped to the United States for dairy purposes have to foe tested for Bang's disease, and they are tested by the government here in order to prevent infected stock going to that country, which in the end might affect our trade with the United States.
So far as the question of destroying the animals is concerned, I do not think there is any regulation at the present time requiring that this should be done. There is a regulation which requires the marking of animals which have been tested and are found to have Bang's disease, in order to safeguard those who may purchase breeding stock, so that they may be protected against purchas-

ing an animal that has this disease. So far, however, no provision has been made for paying for any animals destroyed, and I think I am right in saying that there is no regulation which compels the destruction of these animals.

I believe the minister is right, but the day may come when the government will have to do something in regard to this disease. When the time comes that the government must undertake work of this nature and compel a test, I think for the protection of the live stock industry of this country and also for the protection of the human race, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) pointed out to-day, animals found to be suffering from this disease should be slaughtered and the owners should receive compensation.

I have nothing in particular against the Chinese if they are paid reasonable wages, but the Chinese are employed because they work more cheaply than do Canadians.

I do not see why we should give these huge subsidies to ships of British register, manned

He said:	Mr. Speaker, the bill which I
have introduced and which is before the house this evening has been brought before the house by myself for the fifth time, I believe, since 1930. Having on previous occasions gone very fully into all aspects of the appeal which we in British Columbia have been making for equality in freight rates, it will perhaps not be necessary for me this evening to go as fully into the matter as I have done in former years. Nevertheless it might perhaps be well for me to mention some of the salient points connected with the fight which we in British Columbia are now and have been waging for many long years past.
It might not be amiss for me to say-and I do not believe I am over-optimistic-that we are expecting during the next four or five years some better results than we have had in our fight on this question from 1930 to 1935.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, let me assure you and the house, for the benefit of the new members particularly, that in the appeal which British Columbia is making through the medium of this bill we are not asking for
12739-19J
any special consideration. The people of British Columbia are asking simply that they be granted that equality in the matter of freight rates which has existed in the other provinces since the railways first came into existence.
I would ask you, sir, and also hon. members, why it is that when grain is hauled from Calgary or Edmonton eastward it is designated simply as grain, and yet when similar grain leaves the prairie provinces and heads towards the Pacific coast the railway experts or the railway companies classify it as either grain for export or grain for domestic use. They are, in other words, actually saying to the shippers:	Is this grain going to be consumed in British Columbia? Because if it is we are going to charge you twice the freight rate that we charge the people of Japan or Great Britain for transporting similar or better grain. That, in fact, is what the railways are saying to shippers and users of grain, -and they have persisted in saying it for many, many years.
Now this differentiation and inequality cannot be based upon the ground that it costs more to haul grain into British Columbia than it does to haul grain eastward either to the maritime provinces or to Fort William, for might I point out that the cost of hauling grain into British Columbia is not any greater. As a matter of fact, the actual evidence which was produced in the different appeals which have been heard on this question shows that there is no railway expert competent enough to tell exactly what it costs to haul one ton or one pound of grain.
Then again, there has been in the minds of many people that old story about the mountains; that due to the extra grades and extra engines required, and so forth, the people of British Columbia must necessarily pay a higher freight rate than do the people of the east. I shall not go into that question in detail, but I have before me records to show that not only were construction costs of the railways into British Columbia less than in other parts of the dominion, especially into Fort William, but maintenance and upkeep costs, pusher mileage and all that goes into railway operation are much less in British Columbia than in the eastern provinces. It cannot be too often repeated, that the Canadian National railway line into British Columbia has the lowest grade in the Dominion of Canada. I want to repeat that: The Canadian National railway line into British Columbia is the lowest grade of any in the dominion.

Mountain grade.

grade. I can give the grades if the right hon. leader of the opposition wants them. I can give the grades into Fort William. I am now going to make the strong statement that the freight rate structure of Canada is antiquated and should be thrown overboard. The railway experts in my opinion are actually blocking the progress of this country by always raising the question of through rates, export rates and such like. They do not seem to realize that we are living in a day of progress with motor transport, and the people of this or any other country are not interested in these special arguments that experts bring forward. What the people of this dominion are primarily interested in is how much or how little it will cost them to transport their produce. It is service they are looking for to-day, and I want to repeat that in my opinion the railway experts are just blocking the progress of this country, and indeed, to the detriment of even the railways themselves.
I am glad that at the dominion-provincial conference the transport question was considered. True, it was not the railway problem which we have that was under discussion but the question of transport, and I was pleased to note in the bulletin which was placed in the hands of every member of the house the following recommendation with regard to the regulation of traffic:
That the Minister of Transport arrange to collect information regarding rates prescribed or charged by public carriers of freight and passengers in the various provinces and rates charged by the railway companies and communicate such information to the provinces to the end that a fair and equitable basis_ may be arrived at for the establishing of uniform rates for highway transportation of passengers and freight.
I wonder how the Canadian people would feel if different rates existed in this country for hauling passengers over the same route or over routes of a like distance. Just to show how idiotic some of the freight rates charged are, I shall give the rates on only a few products. Take coal, eggs, butter, dressed poultry, fresh meats and canned goods hauled from Calgary or Edmonton into Vancouver or New Westminster. The rate on

eggs from Edmonton to Vancouver is $1.10, but if a shipper wants to ship back those same eggs from Vancouver to Edmonton over the same route and by the same train, the cost of transport being no greater, he is charged $1.13. And the same is true with regard to butter. The rate from Edmonton to Vancouver is $1.37 per 100 pounds, but if you wanted to ship that back to Edmonton, oh, it would be just too bad, for the railways would say: We will charge you $1.49. And so on down the list. One could mention five hundred different commodities going over the same route and over a like distance where one rate is charged going to the coast and a higher rate coming back. These railway experts have a fine system. They will tell you that that is the through rate, or advance some other argument, and so we find ourselves blocked always by these so-called railway experts.
I shall give only one or two more instances because I have dealt with the matter very fully on previous occasions. I quite realize that this is not the place to make a complete new freight rate structure for this country; I admit that quite frankly. I quoted what I did with a view to bringing home to hon. members a realization of the idiotic, chaotic and archaic system which has been in existence in Canada for many years. I maintain that the continuance of such a system is blocking progress and is hindering trade. I warn the railroads, as I have warned them before, that if they do not wake up and get rid of some of these railroad experts they will find their rail traffic will have completely disappeared and gone into the hands of motor transport companies. The railroads should consider what has been done in other lands, particularly in Great Britain. In that country a great advance has been made during the past year in railway transportation, but here it seems that the railways are not inclined to make any progress. We have the same old system that was in existence in 1867. The people are now, however, demanding a service at a reasonable price and they are not interested in through rates and expert excuses or arguments.

Moreover, as time goes on, they will have to meet more serious competition on the part of the truck. In the first place, the fundamental principles underlying rates on freight for export are not the same as those underlying rates on freight for domestic consumption. If you do not give to the Canadian exporter a rate enabling him to compete in the markets of the world you simply shut him out of those markets. Grain and other products reach foreign markets from various countries where a shorter rail and ocean haul, and sometimes cheaper labour conditions obtain.

traffic must contribute to the overhead and fixed charges of the railway. The same principles do not apply to freight for domestic consumption and freight for export. Freight for export would not move at all unless you publish an export rate; freight for domestic consumption must move even at that higher rate. If you had the same rate structure on goods for domestic consumption and for export you would shift the load from the shoulders of the railway users to those of the general taxpayers of the country. We did our 'best for British Columbia in the course of the general freight rates investigation. We were even accused of having flattened the Rocky mountains. We ordered the railways to publish, on freight moving to Vancouver from any points on the prairies, the same rates as applied to traffic moving for the same distances to Fort William, except that because of competitive conditions, the Canadian Pacific, from Calgary to Vancouver, was authorized to assume the mileage of the Canadian National from Edmonton to Vancouver. The Canadian Pacific had a 2 2 per cent grade in the mountains, as compared with a maximum grade of one per cent on the Canadian National. But they had a shorter mileage of 124 miles. This would have entailed a considerable loss to the two systems.
I therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the rate structure on grain for domestic consumption cannot be predicated upon the same principle as that applying to rates on grain for export, and that the constructive mileage which was permitted to the Canadian Pacific between Calgary and Vancouver is amply justified.

I should like to make this further observation. We have had a great deal of discussion on this particular point, and a number of matters have been raised on which no information can be given at the moment, as to labour conditions, the type of labour employed, whether white or coloured sailors are employed, and to what extent it is necessary to use one class or the other. This afternoon the minister said that it was almost impossible to obtain white labour on these ships. But I would point out that plying from Great Britain to other parts of the world there are ships of similar type manned by white seamen, and consequently I do not think that argument holds good. In view of this very large subsidy that we are being asked to vote, $300,000 a year for two ships sailing to New Zealand, I think this item should stand over until we have more definite information regarding the matters that have been raised and as to the conditions surrounding this subsidy.

I am not sure that any particular purpose will be served by allowing the item to stand for further information. There is no question at all that a good many Chinese are employed on these vessels. Perhaps I can give my hon. friend some of the information he wants now. The total number of Chinese employed on the Empress of

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
Russia and the Empress of Asia is 871. These are the two ships of Canadian registry, the other vessels feeing registered in London. There are about eighty white men employed on each vessel, and on the average a few more than 400 orientals, Chinese.
Has the minister any idea what it would cost to establish a mail service to New Zealand if this steamship service was stopped?
Does my hon. friend mean on government boats?
The minister said this afternoon that if this service wTere to stop it would be necessary to spend some money on a mail service, and I am asking what it would cost approximately.
Does my hon. friend mean what it would cost to put on new boats?
No, merely to establish a mail service in the event of this steamship service being stopped if the subsidy were decreased.

We would probably have to use United States boats, and I do not know what sort of arrangement could be made with them to carry the mails. The cost of carrying the mails on these boats is about $100,000.
Is that in addition to the subsidy?
No, that is included in the subsidy.

Referring to wages and working conditions on these boats for which a subsidy is being asked, evidently the department knows nothing about wages and working conditions, and I do not think it is enough for the minister to say that he will try to have as large a number as possible of white Canadian citizens employed on these boats. I am concerned not only about working conditions but about wages paid on these ships, and I am quite satisfied that if reasonable wages were paid, the class of white labour that could be employed wmuld give the steamship company a much better service than does the class of oriental labour which it is now employing. We are not going to improve conditions by merely substituting low paid white labour for low paid oriental labour. That is not getting us anywhere. When we insist upon working conditions that Canadian citizens, whether they be white, yellow, black, brown or any other colour can accept-I am interested mainly in the fact that they are Canadians-then we shall be getting somewhere. Before this

matter is finally settled I think the minister should be in a position to give us some information as to wages paid and working conditions on these boats.

I am absolutely opposed to the whole idea of subsidies. Members of this government went through the country stating that they were opposed to state intervention; that they believed in individual initiative, in ruthless competition and the law of supply and demand. However, the moment a company finds that it is not in a position to finance itself a request is made to the government for a subsidy of $300,000. When the minister was asked this afternoon as to working conditions aboard these ships he stated that as these two ships were under British registry, he doubted whether we would have any control over them.
The employment of Chinese does not enter into the question of this New Zealand service, which is the one asking for $300,000.

The minister was asked this afternoon as to the wages paid and the type of labour employed by these ships, and he replied that he doubted whether we could control them because they were not Canadian registered. I maintain that no matter what registry they may be under, if they come to parliament asking for a subsidy of $300,000 we should have something to say about the type of people they employ, the wages they pay and the conditions under which they expect men to work. If they are not willing to comply with these requests, I am sure that ships of Canadian registry could be found to take over the service.

Mr. Chairman, before the
committee rose at six o'clock a suggestion was made to the minister that it be made a condition of subsidies granted to ocean going steamers that they hire Canadian sailors. This suggestion seemed to receive support from many hon. members. It is a policy which would be most advantageous to the maritime sections of Canada. Since I entered the house I have heard it said many times by members of every shade of opinion that the greatest problem facing this country is unemployment. I represent Queens-Lunenburg, a typical maritime constituency. While central Canada has a problem of unemployment in its cities, our problem is one of finding employment for our seamen. Most of our men have followed the sea since their childhood, and it seems to me that when we are considering unemployment we should consider the sailors who go down to the sea in ships. This matter has received
